strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of MLLMs in medical diagnosis (quantitative analysis, hallucinations)
Strong empirical results on tested benchmarks: 90.4% mACC on glaucoma, outperforms REFUGE2 winners (95.1 AUC vs 88.3)
Clear system design with hierarchical two-level architecture and focus on interpretability/evidence-based diagnosis
Comprehensive experiments including comparisons with multiple baseline types, ablation studies, and case studies
Practical approach that doesn't require fine-tuning of MLLMs
Clear presentation with helpful visualizations of system architecture
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RAG for medical documents, hierarchical agent decomposition, and MOE decider are straightforward applications of existing techniques; the simple weighted-sum formulation (Eq. 1-2) is not novel
Severely narrow evaluation scope: only 2 diseases tested (glaucoma and heart disease); heart disease simplified from 7-class to binary classification, limiting clinical relevance
Missing clinical validation: no human evaluation with physicians, no failure case analysis, no statistical significance testing despite being a medical system

System design requires manual configuration: MOE weights and thresholds must be set per disease with no principled learning approach; task-specific tool agents (RetiZero, VisionUnite adapters) needed for each disease

Unfair baseline comparisons: comparing zero-shot MedAgent-Pro against fine-tuned task-specific models conflates system performance with tool quality; 3D handling (randomly select 3 slices, average 10 times) is a workaround
Generalization concerns: strong evidence of task-specific engineering; unclear how to set up system for new diseases without significant domain expertise and tool curation

Reproducibility issues: missing implementation details (RAG construction, exact prompts, weight determination procedure); promised code repository not provided; no details on how missing modalities are handled
Indicator reliability not addressed: Table 3 shows poor-performing indicators (DH) still included; no mechanism for adaptive tool quality handling
Incomplete evaluation: no ablation on RAG value, no cross-disease generalization testing, no computational cost analysis, no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (weights, thresholds)
Overclaimed novelty: statements like 'state-of-the-art' based only on 2 diseases; insufficient discussion of differences from recent similar systems (MmedAgent, MedRax)

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing evaluation across 4 datasets, 50+ diseases, 10+ imaging modalities, and 20+ anatomies with significant improvements over baselines (34% over GPT-4o on glaucoma)
Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in prior work (VLMs as one-hop QA vs. structured clinical reasoning)
Principled hierarchical architecture mirroring real clinical workflows (disease-level planning + patient-level reasoning)
Practical design integrating RAG for guideline retrieval and specialized visual tools for quantitative analysis
Clinician evaluation on multiple output quality dimensions (relevance, comprehensiveness, reliability, coherence, clarity)
Strong empirical results outperforming not only general VLMs but also SOTA task-specific models
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and compelling clinical examples
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily an engineering contribution combining well-established techniques (RAG, hierarchical reasoning, tool integration) rather than novel methodologies
Overstated 'evidence-based reasoning' claims: verification still relies on VLM judgment (Eq. 4), not independent clinical evidence; term 'evidence-based' misuses medical terminology
Critical architectural details underspecified: weight assignment (Eq. 5) mechanism unclear, state assessment function φ treated as black box, orchestration process vague
Significant dependence on tool availability with limited exploration of graceful degradation; NEJM results show substantial performance drop and tool-free cases not clearly analyzed
Ablation study gaps: no RAG ablation, limited evidence-based reasoning ablation, no exploration of alternative fusion strategies or knowledge base sensitivity
Reproducibility concerns: no code release, critical prompts not provided, threshold settings unexplained, insufficient implementation details for orchestration and tool selection
Experimental design issues: MITEA uses random 3-slice selection from 3D images (suboptimal), baseline adaptation fairness questionable, potential data leakage in MIMIC splits not addressed
Human evaluation limitations: only 2 domains (glaucoma, chest X-ray), sample sizes unclear, inter-rater reliability not reported, evaluation on output quality not diagnostic accuracy
Circular verification problem: same or similar VLMs verifying each other's outputs without truly independent evidence
Generalization concerns: unclear how framework handles rare diseases or complex cases without clear diagnostic pathways; performance on real-world NEJM dataset notably lower
